title: OVER and PARTITION BY: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD
summary: A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, its partition, and keeps every row: aggregates with OVER, rankings with row_number/rank/dense_rank, neighbours with lag/lead. Windows run after WHERE and GROUP BY, so filtering on one takes a subquery.

examples.title: Aggregates OVER (PARTITION BY ...): group figures without losing the rows

annotations.note: The baseline: GROUP BY answers "per suite" with one row per suite, and the individual tests are no longer in the result.

Each OVER (PARTITION BY suite) aggregate sees the rows of its own suite and writes the result onto every one of them: five rows in, five rows out. OVER () makes the whole result one partition, so all_ms is the grand total on every row.
A row's share of its group in one pass. Without windows this needs a join back to a grouped subquery. 100.0 keeps the division numeric; with integers, 100 * 80 / 600 would print 13 instead of 13.3.

The inner query computes suite_avg for every row; the outer query sees it as an ordinary column and can filter on it. A CTE works the same way. PostgreSQL has no clause for filtering window results in place.

SQLSTATE 42P20. Logically FROM and WHERE run first, then GROUP BY and HAVING, then the window functions, then DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT. When WHERE runs, there is no average yet. The same rule forbids window functions in GROUP BY and HAVING.

examples.title: row_number, rank and dense_rank on ties, and named windows

annotations.note: Three auth tests take 300 ms. To a window ordered by duration they are peers: rows its ORDER BY can't tell apart. Ties are where the three ranking functions differ.

rank gives peers the same number and then skips: 1, 2, 2, 2, 5. dense_rank doesn't skip, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3: it counts distinct durations. Both are fully determined by the data, so they need no tie-breaker.

row_number always counts 1, 2, 3, so the peers must be put in some order. Without the title the docs say tied rows are numbered in an unspecified order, and the numbers can move between runs. COLLATE "tr-x-icu" sorts the tie Turkish-alphabetically, Çıkış before Giriş; the database default C.UTF-8 compares code points and would put Ç after O.

The WINDOW clause names a definition once. by_time copies per_suite's PARTITION BY and adds an ORDER BY; the row_number call does the same with a longer ORDER BY. A copy may add an ORDER BY only if the original has none, and never its own PARTITION BY.

Windows run after GROUP BY, so they see one row per suite, and their ORDER BY may use an aggregate: the suites ranked by total time. An aggregate inside a window is fine; a window inside an aggregate is not.

examples.title: lag and lead: compare each run with the previous and next run

annotations.note: ran_at::date and the printed timestamps depend on the session time zone; pinning it keeps the output the same on every server.
PARTITION BY test_case keeps the two histories apart: lag never reaches into another test's runs. ORDER BY ran_at defines "previous"; id breaks a tie between two runs started in the same instant.
lag looks one row back. On a test's first run there is no such row, so it returns NULL, or the third argument when you give one. lag(status, 2) would look two rows back.
Arithmetic on a neighbour's value: the 940 ms failure shows up as +810 against the day before, and the recovery as -815.
lead looks forward. timestamptz minus timestamptz is an interval ('1 day', '1 day 14:35:00'), and each test's last run has no next run, hence NULL.

Like any window result, prev can only be filtered one level up. The passed-then-failed transitions are regressions: Giriş on 11-12. Çıkış has never passed, so it never regressed; finding how long it has been red is the gaps-and-islands lesson.

use_cases: A row's share of its group: each test's share of its suite's time, each order's share of the customer's revenue
Rankings inside groups: slowest tests per suite, leaderboard positions with ties (rank, dense_rank)
Comparing a row with its neighbour: duration change since the previous run, passed-to-failed transitions, time between events (lag, lead)
Numbering rows to keep one per key: deduplication and latest-row-per-key with row_number() = 1
strengths: Detail rows and group figures in one result: nothing is collapsed as with GROUP BY, and unlike a join back to a grouped subquery the table is read once
lag and lead compare a row with its neighbour in the query itself, where application code would sort, group and track a `prev` variable by hand
rank and dense_rank define what happens to ties, so a leaderboard doesn't depend on the order rows happen to arrive in
Window functions are standard SQL, unlike DISTINCT ON, so the row_number() form of 'first row per group' is portable
weaknesses: Window results can't be filtered at the same query level: every 'keep rank <= 3' needs a subquery or CTE
row_number over a non-unique ORDER BY returns arbitrary numbers for ties, and nothing warns you
Windows with different PARTITION BY or ORDER BY typically need a sort each; several unrelated windows in one query mean several sorts
PostgreSQL doesn't implement the standard's IGNORE NULLS option, so 'the previous non-NULL value' takes extra work

pitfalls.title: A window function in WHERE
pitfalls.detail: WHERE is evaluated before window functions exist (SQLSTATE 42P20). Compute the value in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT * FROM test_runs WHERE row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY id) = 1
pitfalls.good: SELECT * FROM (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM test_runs) AS t WHERE rn = 1

pitfalls.title: row_number without a unique ORDER BY
pitfalls.detail: Peers are numbered in an unspecified order, so 'the first row' can differ between runs. End the window's ORDER BY with a unique column.
pitfalls.bad: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC)
pitfalls.good: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC, id)

pitfalls.title: lag without PARTITION BY
pitfalls.detail: Without a partition, the 'previous run' of one test's first run is the last run of some other test, and the transition looks real.
pitfalls.good: lag(status) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at, id)

pitfalls.title: Expecting the window's ORDER BY to sort the result
pitfalls.detail: It orders the rows inside the computation. The output happens to follow some window's sort today, and the docs say not to rely on it. Write the query's own ORDER BY.

pitfalls.title: Adding ORDER BY to an aggregate's window
pitfalls.detail: sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY s) is the group total; sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY s ORDER BY t) is a running total, because ORDER BY also changes the default frame. The next lesson covers frames.

quiz.q: Durations, slowest first: 500, 300, 300, 200. What do rank() and dense_rank() give the 200 ms test?
quiz.why: rank skips after a tie (1, 2, 2, 4); dense_rank doesn't (1, 2, 2, 3).

quiz.q: Why does `SELECT * FROM t WHERE rank() OVER (ORDER BY x) <= 3` fail?
options: Window functions are computed after WHERE, so WHERE can't use them
rank() is only allowed together with GROUP BY
quiz.why: Windows are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING; they're allowed only in the SELECT list and ORDER BY. Filter in an outer query.

quiz.q: What does `lag(status) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at)` return on a test case's first run?
options: The last status of the previous test case
quiz.why: lag never crosses a partition boundary; with no row before, it returns its default, which is NULL unless you pass a third argument.

quiz.q: What does `sum(duration_ms) OVER ()` put on each row?
options: The total over all rows the query kept after WHERE
NULL, because there is no PARTITION BY
quiz.why: An empty OVER () makes all rows one partition, and with no ORDER BY the frame is the whole partition.

body:
## Concept

A **window function** computes a value for each row from a set of rows related to it,
and unlike `GROUP BY` it returns every row. Writing `OVER (...)` after a call makes it
a window call:

- `PARTITION BY` splits the rows into groups. A window function never looks outside
  the current row's partition; without `PARTITION BY` the whole result is one partition.
- `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` orders the rows within each partition. It defines what
  "previous" and "first" mean and how ranks are assigned. It does not sort the output.

Three families of functions use it:

- **Any aggregate** (`sum`, `count`, `avg`, ...) followed by `OVER`: the group's
  figure, written onto each of its rows.
- **Ranking:** `row_number()` counts 1, 2, 3, ... no matter what; `rank()` gives ties
  the same number and then skips (1, 2, 2, 4); `dense_rank()` gives ties the same
  number without skipping (1, 2, 2, 3).
- **Offsets:** `lag(x, n, default)` and `lead(x, n, default)` read `x` from the row `n`
  positions before or after the current one, within the partition.

Window functions are evaluated after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, and before
`DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`. They are allowed only in the `SELECT` list and the
query's `ORDER BY`; to filter on one, compute it in a subquery or CTE.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python (pandas):** `df.groupby('suite')['ms'].transform('sum')` is
  `sum(ms) OVER (PARTITION BY suite)`: a group value broadcast back onto each row.
  `groupby(...).rank(method='min')`, `method='dense'` and `method='first'` are `rank`,
  `dense_rank` and `row_number`; `groupby(...).shift(1)` is `lag`.
- **Java, JS, Go:** there is no built-in equivalent. You would group rows into a map
  of lists, sort each list, then loop with an index and a `prev` variable. The window
  does the grouping, the sort and the reset at each group boundary for you.
- **C/C++:** `lag` and `lead` are the `a[i-1]` and `a[i+1]` of a loop over a sorted
  array, with a bounds check that returns a default, restarted for every group.
- **Everyone:** the window's `ORDER BY` is not the result's `ORDER BY`. It decides the
  computation, like the comparator you pass to a sort inside a group-by. The output
  order is set only by the query's own `ORDER BY`.

## How it works

The executor sorts the rows by the partition and order columns and walks them once in
a `WindowAgg` step, resetting its state at each partition boundary. Window functions
with equivalent `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY` share that pass, and the docs guarantee
they see the same row order even when the `ORDER BY` has ties. A window with a
different definition typically needs another sort, and that sort is not guaranteed to
keep tied rows in the same order: one more reason to make `row_number`'s order unique.

The order of evaluation explains the restrictions. Rows are filtered (`WHERE`), grouped
(`GROUP BY`, `HAVING`), and only then windowed. So a window may rank groups by an
aggregate (example 2), but `WHERE` and `HAVING` can never see a window's result.

## Design notes

Use `GROUP BY` when you want one row per group, and a window when you need the detail
rows and the group figures together, or a row compared with its neighbour. `lag` and
`lead` replace the old self-join on "the previous row", which needed a correlated
`max(ran_at) ... < r.ran_at` lookup per row.

Pick the ranking function by what a tie should mean. `rank` or `dense_rank` when ties
must stay visible (a leaderboard, "the slowest tests" where two are equally slow);
`row_number` with a unique tie-breaker when you need exactly one row per position
(deduplication, "the latest run per test").

Filters belong on one side of the window or the other, on purpose. A condition in
`WHERE` changes what the window sees: `WHERE status = 'failed'` before `lag` makes
"previous" mean "previous failure". A condition on the window's result goes in the
outer query. Name shared definitions in a `WINDOW` clause, so several functions
provably use the same partition and order.

files.examples/01_partition.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.windows.over): a window function computes over related rows and keeps every row.
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int  PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  test_case   text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int  NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'Giriş',            120),
  (2, 'auth',   'Çıkış',             80),
  (3, 'auth',   'Şifre sıfırlama',  400),
  (4, 'export', 'CSV dışa aktarım', 900),
  (5, 'export', 'PDF rapor',        300);

-- GROUP BY collapses each suite into one row; the tests are gone.
SELECT suite, count(*) AS runs, sum(duration_ms) AS suite_ms
FROM test_runs
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- The same aggregates with OVER keep every row and attach the group's figures.
SELECT suite, test_case, duration_ms,
       count(*)         OVER (PARTITION BY suite) AS runs,
       sum(duration_ms) OVER (PARTITION BY suite) AS suite_ms,
       round(100.0 * duration_ms / sum(duration_ms) OVER (PARTITION BY suite), 1)
                                                  AS pct_of_suite,
       sum(duration_ms) OVER ()                   AS all_ms
FROM test_runs
ORDER BY suite, id;

-- Filtering on a window result needs a subquery: compute first, filter outside.
SELECT suite, test_case, duration_ms, suite_avg
FROM (
  SELECT suite, test_case, duration_ms,
         round(avg(duration_ms) OVER (PARTITION BY suite)) AS suite_avg
  FROM test_runs
) AS t
WHERE duration_ms > suite_avg
ORDER BY suite, test_case;

-- WHERE runs before any window is computed, so it can't refer to one.
SELECT test_case FROM test_runs
WHERE duration_ms > avg(duration_ms) OVER (PARTITION BY suite);
files.examples/02_ranking.sql:
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id          int  PRIMARY KEY,
  suite       text NOT NULL,
  title       text NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int  NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'Oturum süresi',        300),
  (2, 'auth',   'Giriş',                300),
  (3, 'auth',   'İki adımlı doğrulama', 500),
  (4, 'auth',   'Çıkış',                300),
  (5, 'auth',   'Şifre sıfırlama',      200),
  (6, 'export', 'CSV dışa aktarım',     900),
  (7, 'export', 'PDF rapor',            900);

-- Slowest first in each suite. Three tests tie at 300 ms: rank and
-- dense_rank give them one number, row_number needs a tie-breaker.
SELECT suite, title, duration_ms,
       rank()       OVER by_time AS rank,
       dense_rank() OVER by_time AS dense_rank,
       row_number() OVER (per_suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC,
                          title COLLATE "tr-x-icu") AS row_number
FROM test_cases
WINDOW per_suite AS (PARTITION BY suite),
       by_time   AS (per_suite ORDER BY duration_ms DESC)
ORDER BY suite, row_number;

-- Windows run after GROUP BY, so they can rank the groups themselves.
SELECT suite, sum(duration_ms) AS suite_ms,
       rank() OVER (ORDER BY sum(duration_ms) DESC) AS slowest
FROM test_cases
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY slowest, suite;
files.examples/03_lag_lead.sql:
SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id          int         PRIMARY KEY,
  test_case   text        NOT NULL,
  ran_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
  status      text        NOT NULL,
  duration_ms int         NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES
  (1, 'Giriş', '2026-11-10 09:00+03', 'passed', 120),
  (2, 'Giriş', '2026-11-11 09:00+03', 'passed', 130),
  (3, 'Giriş', '2026-11-12 09:00+03', 'failed', 940),
  (4, 'Giriş', '2026-11-13 09:00+03', 'passed', 125),
  (5, 'Çıkış', '2026-11-11 18:30+03', 'failed',  80),
  (6, 'Çıkış', '2026-11-13 09:05+03', 'failed',  85);

-- Each run next to the previous and next run of the same test case.
SELECT test_case, ran_at::date AS day, status,
       lag(status) OVER w                    AS prev_status,
       lag(status, 1, 'first run') OVER w    AS prev_or_label,
       duration_ms - lag(duration_ms) OVER w AS delta_ms,
       lead(ran_at) OVER w - ran_at          AS until_next_run
FROM test_runs
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at, id)
ORDER BY test_case, ran_at, id;

-- Regressions: a run that failed right after a pass of the same test.
SELECT test_case, ran_at
FROM (
  SELECT test_case, ran_at, status,
         lag(status) OVER (PARTITION BY test_case ORDER BY ran_at, id) AS prev
  FROM test_runs
) AS r
WHERE prev = 'passed' AND status = 'failed'
ORDER BY ran_at;
